case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourline Urban Lines (HUL) is a private limited company in the passenger transport sector, employing a workforce of 45. Founded in 2005 by Grace Mensah, the business runs coastal coach services for commuters and tourists and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HUL plans to invest $960,000 in a fleet of low-emission coaches, financed by a $650,000 bank loan and $310,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently carries 62,000 units a year. HUL faces two operational problems: driver absenteeism has reached 11% and rising vehicle defects are causing punctuality complaints from passengers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The coach fleet completed 15,800 journeys last month with a defect-related delay rate of 4.4%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Passenger complaints fell from 85 to 49 per month. Average journey delay is 6.2 minutes. A survey of 700 passengers found that 64% would pay up to $0.40 more for guaranteed on-time, low-emission travel, and 59% check an operator's environmental record before booking. A training needs analysis shows 16 of 45 drivers lack low-emission vehicle skills; on-the-job training is available, while off-the-job training at the local college costs $780 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourline Urban Lines for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $13.00 to $13.75 per hour from April 2026, raising driver wage bills. (3) Diesel and energy input costs rose 10.8% year-on-year, tourism bookings grew 5.6%, and household consumer spending fell 0.9%.

questions.question_text: HUL plans to fund part of its $960,000 low-emission coach fleet with $310,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HUL of using retained profit rather than increasing its $650,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or capital repayment, so using the $310,000 protects HUL's cash flow while it already services a $650,000 bank loan and faces fixed costs of $360,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 10.8% rise in diesel and energy costs, helping HUL hold its $15.00 fare and remain competitive with other coastal operators.

Point 2: Retaining profit avoids further collateral and the risk of coaches being repossessed if tourism bookings fall, and it preserves Grace Mensah's control of the private limited company. No lender can impose conditions on how the $960,000 fleet is deployed, so management can respond flexibly to the 11% driver absenteeism and the 4.4% defect-related delay rate without seeking a bank's approval. With 2024 revenue of $2,600,000 in Appendix 2, HUL has a solid profit base to release $310,000 internally. The $310,000 also reduces reliance on external finance as the 5.00% base rate rises.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to HUL and its coach-fleet financing decision.

questions.question_text: HUL is promoting its guaranteed on-time, low-emission coach travel. Consider a national television campaign, local radio advertising, or partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations. Which should HUL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would build rapid, broad awareness of low-emission travel, but airtime and production costs are very high and most viewers are not potential coastal passengers. For a 45-employee operator funding a $960,000 fleet and a $650,000 loan, most of the spend would be wasted and few of the 700 surveyed passengers would be reached.

Local radio advertising: Local radio is much cheaper and can target the coastal communities HUL serves, carrying a simple punctuality message to drivers near its routes. However, its reach is limited to one region and cannot build a wider brand; the 64% of surveyed passengers willing to pay $0.40 more for on-time, low-emission travel include tourists from beyond the local area.

Partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations: Working with tourist boards, employers and commuter groups targets exactly the passengers who value reliable, low-emission travel, using the $0.40 premium in joint offers and measuring take-up through bookings. The 59% who check an operator's environmental record can be shown the new fleet's credentials directly, at low cost.

Recommendation: HUL should choose partnerships with tourism and commuter organisations. This reaches the precise segments in the survey, costs far less than television and delivers measurable bookings. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted given the $650,000 loan; local radio is rejected as too narrow for a service that attracts tourists from outside the region, though short radio bursts can support the partnerships. HUL can also publicise the new low-emission fleet alongside the 5.6% growth in tourism bookings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HUL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HUL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HUL's driver absenteeism has reached 11% and it uses democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for HUL of democratic leadership in reducing absenteeism among its drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HUL's workforce of 45 a genuine voice in how the new low-emission coach fleet and duty rosters are organised, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Drivers who help design schedules and rest arrangements are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 11% absenteeism that disrupts the 62,000-unit service.

Point 2: Consulting drivers generates practical ideas for cutting the 4.4% defect-related delays and punctuality complaints, since they drive the routes daily. Greater involvement raises commitment, lowers labour turnover and saves the $780 per driver retraining cost, protecting service quality as the $960,000 fleet arrives. Better morale also supports the on-time reliability that 64% of surveyed passengers value and the environmental record 59% check before booking. The defect-related delay rate has already fallen from 6.1% to 4.4%, showing that engaged drivers can improve punctuality as the new coaches arrive. Keeping experienced drivers also protects the 6.2-minute average delay the service is trying to cut.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HUL's absenteeism, punctuality and output.

questions.question_text: HUL must train 16 drivers to operate the new low-emission coaches. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should HUL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on the actual coaches and routes is directly relevant to HUL's operations, costs no course fees, and keeps the 16 drivers productive while they learn, protecting the 62,000-unit service and the drive to cut the 4.4% defect-related delay rate. However, trainers are working drivers whose own journeys suffer, bad habits can spread, and there is no formal certificate if regulators or partners ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $780 per driver gives structured low-emission vehicle knowledge and a recognised certificate for all 16, costing $12,480 in total — modest against the $960,000 fleet. It removes drivers from the road, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match HUL's exact routes, so depot follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: HUL should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college sessions for senior drivers. It is cheapest, vehicle-specific and avoids further capacity loss while absenteeism is already 11%; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $12,480 and releasing 16 drivers would reduce service frequency on coastal routes, and college modules can be added once the fleet is running reliably and the 4.4% delay rate falls. With 15,800 journeys completed last month and complaints still at 49, releasing 16 drivers would cut service frequency when passengers value punctuality. On-the-job training protects the 62,000-unit service, and the $12,480 saved could fund short college certificates once the fleet is bedded in. Senior drivers can later cascade the skills to the rest of the fleet, helping sustain the on-time, low-emission service that 64% of passengers value.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HUL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HUL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HUL with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HUL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($15.00 − $7.50) = $360,000 ÷ $7.50 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 − $7.50 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HUL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 62,000 units gives a margin of safety of 14,000 units, confirming the coach operation is profitable and supporting the $960,000 low-emission fleet investment.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.50 lets managers model the $0.40 premium from the passenger survey: if offered as a discount instead, contribution would fall to $7.10 and break-even would rise to about 50,704 units ($360,000 ÷ $7.10), so extra passengers must be carried.
3. With fixed costs of $360,000, managers can set the passenger volume needed to service the $650,000 bank loan and check that 62,000 units covers it before borrowing more.
4. Unit cost data ($360,000 ÷ 62,000 units + $7.50 = $13.31 a unit) can be benchmarked monthly to detect the 4.4% defect-related delays and to judge whether the 10.8% diesel and energy rise is being absorbed without cutting the $7.50 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 14,000 units against 62,000 output; discount modelling with $0.40 and $7.10 contribution; loan servicing against $360,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $13.31 to tackle delays.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate the profitability of HUL by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has HUL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $1,040,000 on revenue of $2,600,000 compares with 2025 gross profit of $1,320,000 on revenue of $3,000,000; cost of sales rose only from $1,560,000 to $1,680,000 while revenue grew faster. Operating profit increased from $312,000 to $420,000, and capital employed from $1,950,000 to $2,400,000; interest payable rose from $42,000 to $58,000 but stays modest.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The 40.0% to 44.0% change shows HUL kept more of each revenue dollar after direct operating costs, so the 10.8% diesel and energy shock was partly passed on through the $15.00 fare and the 5.6% growth in tourism bookings. The 12.0% to 14.0% operating result shows overhead control as the business expanded, and the 16.0% to 17.5% return on capital employed shows the asset base generated more operating profit even while the $960,000 fleet was being funded. Interest payable remains small relative to operating profit, so the $650,000 loan is manageable. The caution is that capital employed grew faster than the return, and household spending fell 0.9%, so future passenger demand cannot be assumed.

Conclusion: HUL's financial performance has improved. Gross margin, operating margin and return on capital employed all rose together between 2024 and 2025, showing broad-based progress rather than a one-off gain. HUL should proceed with the $960,000 fleet while monitoring that the new capital earns comparable returns and that the 11% absenteeism and 4.4% delays are reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three profitability ratios for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margins, operating profit and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HUL of guaranteeing on-time, low-emission coach travel.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 700 passengers found 64% would pay up to $0.40 more for guaranteed on-time, low-emission travel, so HUL can add a premium that protects its $7.50 contribution per unit while diesel and energy costs rise 10.8%. It also appeals to the 59% who check an operator's environmental record, helping win passengers and the 5.6% growth in tourism bookings needed to justify the $960,000 fleet.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing punctuality requires reliable vehicles and spare capacity, which could push up the $360,000 fixed costs and the $7.50 variable cost per unit. With vehicle-defect delays at 4.4% and absenteeism at 11%, any failure would trigger refunds and damage HUL's reputation. The $650,000 loan leaves limited room to fund a costly guarantee, and passengers may demand it without accepting the full $0.40 premium on every journey. The 4.4% delay rate makes any punctuality promise hard to honour without first improving reliability. Refunds would also cut the $7.50 contribution on affected journeys.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HUL's survey data, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in diesel and energy input costs will affect HUL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 5.00%): If HUL's $650,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 1.00% of $650,000 = $6,500 a year (0.01 × $650,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $360,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also caution passengers and raise future borrowing costs, but HUL can largely remove this risk by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.75 per hour): HUL employs a workforce of 45, with many drivers likely paid hourly, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 62,000 units ÷ 45 staff = about 1,378 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism at 11% lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $7.50 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Diesel and energy inputs (10.8%): HUL's variable cost of $7.50 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% it would add 10.8% × $7.50 = $0.81 per unit, and at 62,000 units that is about $50,000 a year (62,000 × $0.81). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $7.50 contribution materially. HUL can offset part through the $0.40 on-time premium in the survey.

Conclusion: The 10.8% diesel and energy rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 62,000 passenger units and directly erodes the $7.50 contribution that supports the $960,000 fleet. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. HUL should secure the $0.40 premium and improve fuel efficiency to protect margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HUL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HUL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HUL with a well-justified judgment that energy costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
